My lord may prepare gifts for presentation, and I shall go personally to Xudu and persuade Cao Cao to raise an army against Hanzhong and attack Zhang Lu. Then Zhang Lu will be too occupied resisting his enemy to dare cast another covetous eye upon Shu.” Liu Zhang was delighted. He assembled gold, pearls, brocades, and fine silks as gifts and dispatched Zhang Song as his envoy. Zhang Song secretly drew a map of the geography of Sichuan and concealed it on his person; then, accompanied by several mounted attendants, he took the road to Xudu. Ever since returning from his victory over Ma Chao, Cao Cao had been proud and complacent. p.src: Zhang Song looked at the man. He had a single continuous brow, narrow eyes, a fair complexion, and a lucid bearing. He was widely learned and eloquent, with insight surpassing that of ordinary men. Zhang Song knew Yang Xiu to be a master of debate and deliberately sought to confound him. Yang Xiu, for his part, relied upon his own talents and looked down upon all the scholars of the realm. Hearing Zhang Song’s mocking words, Yang Xiu invited him to a study outside. They seated themselves as host and guest, and Yang Xiu said, “The roads of Shu are rugged; you must have suffered greatly on your long journey.” Zhang Song replied, “Charged with my lord’s command, I would not shrink even from boiling water or blazing fire.” Yang Xiu asked, “What are the land and customs of Shu like?” Zhang Song replied, “Shu is a western commandery, known in ancient times as Yizhou. Its roads are guarded by the perilous Jin River, and its lands adjoin the mighty fastness of Jiange. Its circuit comprises two hundred and eight stages, and it extends more than thirty thousand li in every direction. The crowing of cocks and barking of dogs carry from village to village, while markets and dwellings stretch on without end. The fields are fertile and the soil is rich, and no year brings fear of flood or drought; the state is wealthy and the people prosperous, and music of strings and pipes is heard in every season. Its produce is abundant, heaped as high as mountains. Nothing beneath Heaven can compare with it!”

p.src: The next day, Yang Xiu accompanied Zhang Song to the western drill ground. Cao Cao reviewed fifty thousand stalwart soldiers of the Tiger Guard arrayed across the field; their helmets and armor gleamed, and their robes shone brilliantly. Gongs and drums shook the heavens, while spears and halberds flashed in the sun. Companies were drawn up on every side. Banners streamed in splendid colors, and men and horses surged as though taking flight. Zhang Song regarded it all from the corner of his eye. After a long while, Cao Cao summoned Zhang Song, pointed out the troops, and said, “Have you ever seen such heroes in your land of Shu?” Zhang Song replied, “In our Shu we have never seen such weapons of war; we govern the people only through benevolence and righteousness.” Cao Cao’s expression changed as he stared at him. Zhang Song showed no fear at all, though Yang Xiu repeatedly signaled him with his eyes. Cao Cao said to Zhang Song, “In my eyes, the vermin of the realm are no more than weeds. Wherever my great army goes, it wins every battle and takes every stronghold. Those who submit to me live; those who oppose me die. Do you understand?” Zhang Song replied, “I have long known that wherever the Prime Minister leads his troops, every battle is won and every place attacked is taken. As when you attacked Lü Bu at Puyang, or fought Zhang Xiu at Wancheng; when you met Zhou Yu at the Red Cliffs, or encountered Guan Yu at Huarong; when at Tong Pass you cut off your beard and cast away your robe, or on the Wei River seized a boat to escape the arrows—each of these indeed showed you unrivaled under Heaven.” Cao Cao flew into a rage. “How dare a wretched pedant expose my failures!” He shouted for his attendants to drag Zhang Song away and behead him. Yang Xiu remonstrated, “Zhang Song may deserve death, but he has come all the way from Shu to present tribute. If he is executed, I fear it will estrange people from distant lands.” Cao Cao’s anger had not yet subsided. Xun Yu also remonstrated, and only then did Cao Cao spare Zhang Song’s life, ordering instead that he be beaten out with a flurry of cudgels.

In the winter of that year, he led the army toward the Western River. After only a few stages, Meng Da came to meet him, paid his respects, and said that Governor Liu had ordered him to come from afar with five thousand troops to welcome Xuande. Xuande sent a messenger into Yizhou to notify Liu Zhang in advance. Liu Zhang then issued letters to the prefectures and commanderies along the route, ordering them to supply money and provisions. Wishing to go personally to Fu City to receive Xuande, Liu Zhang ordered carriages and canopies, banners and armor to be prepared, all of them splendid and bright. The registrar Huang Quan remonstrated: “If you go, my lord, Liu Bei will surely do you harm. I have received your stipend for many years and cannot bear to see you fall victim to another’s treacherous scheme. I beg you to reconsider.” Zhang Song said, “Huang Quan’s words estrange the bonds of kinship and magnify the power of our enemies. They are truly of no benefit to my lord.” Liu Zhang rebuked Huang Quan: “My mind is made up. Why do you oppose me?” Huang Quan knocked his head upon the floor until it bled, then came forward and caught Liu Zhang’s robe in his teeth as he continued to remonstrate. Liu Zhang flew into a rage and rose, wrenching at his robe. Huang Quan would not let go, and two of his front teeth were torn out. Liu Zhang shouted to his attendants to drag Huang Quan out, and Huang Quan returned home weeping bitterly.
